title: When the owner pronoun can be left out
focus: First- and second-person endings already identify the owner, so minun, sinun, meidän, and teidän can be omitted: minun palloni or palloni both mean “my ball”.
targetSkills: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference

exercises.prompt: Choose “my ball” without the owner pronoun. Use minun palloni (“my ball”).
exercises.explanation: Remove only minun; keep palloni. The -ni ending identifies the owner.
requiredSkills: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference
exercises.targetSkill: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference
exercises.misconceptionCategory: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference: form or meaning confused

optionFeedback.minun pallo: This removes the noun ending rather than the pronoun.
optionFeedback.pallo: The basic noun alone no longer identifies its owner.

exercises.prompt: Write “This is my pen.” in Finnish. Use tämä (“this”), on (“is”), and minun kynäni (“my pen”). The owner pronoun is optional.
exercises.explanation: The ending on kynäni already identifies the owner, so both the pronoun-free and explicit-pronoun sentences are natural.
requiredSkills: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference
exercises.targetSkill: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference
exercises.misconceptionCategory: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference: form or meaning confused

sentenceExplanation.pattern: tämä + on + noun with possessive ending

parts.formation: Tämä is the supplied basic singular word for “this”.
Olla uses on because the thing being identified is singular; the owner can still be plural.
kynä + -ni = kynäni. The ending marks the owner, not several things.

answerDiagnostics.category: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference: predictable form error
answerDiagnostics.explanation: In standard written Finnish, omitting the pronoun is possible here; omitting the possessive noun ending is not.

The shared third-person ending cannot distinguish his/her from their in this identity frame; retain the pronoun.
The shared suffix alone leaves this third-person owner unclear.
This pronoun changes the reference between one owner and several.

sentenceExplanation.pattern: tämä + on + genitive owner pronoun + noun with matching possessive ending

parts.formation: Tämä is the supplied basic singular word for “this”.
Olla uses on because the thing being identified is singular; the owner can still be plural.
Use the learned genitive form: hänen. Genitive means the form naming whose thing it is.
kissa + -nsa = kissansa. The ending marks the owner, not several things.
